scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Eccentric dance developed as a recognized genre in the United States during the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
It arose from the dynamic collision of traditional European-derived clog and tap dancing with the expressive freedom and rhythmic character of African and exotic dance traditions.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Conceived for public entertainment and variety performance, eccentric dance provided comic relief, character illustration, and technical novelty.
It celebrated individual style, physical humor, and the deliberate defiance of polite, codified movement norms, offering audiences a release into joyful, absurd, and anti-classical physicality.
Today it is a historical tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Eccentric dance is danced through unconventional, individualistic, and exaggerated physical comedy.
Instead of holding the body stiff and straight in the traditional manner of a jig, dancers deliberately isolate body segments, shaking or snaking their limbs in styles termed rubber legs or legmania.
Watch for Rubber legs, Legmania, Torso disassociation.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Eccentric dance accompanied early jazz, novelty music, vaudeville pit orchestra numbers, and Broadway comic songs.
Brian Harker's musicological research links early eccentric dance closely to the evolution of jazz and the pioneering playing of figures like Louis Armstrong on the eve of swing.
Listen for the orchestral brass, woodwinds, percussion, pit band instrumentation.

Vaudeville-era pit orchestration, ragtime, or early jazz characterized by buoyant theatrical rhythms, sudden dynamic comic hits, and syncopated brass and percussion designed to punctuate falls, kicks, and visual physical gags.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The dance was performed in vaudeville theatres, music halls, Broadway stages, and soundstages for cinematic comedies.

Costumes typically emphasized physical humor, visual distortion, and character archetypes, ranging from baggy street clothes and exaggerated comic suits to theatrical stage outfits like Ray Bolger's floppy straw-filled Scarecrow costume in The Wizard of Oz.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Prominent performers historically categorized as eccentric dancers include Ray Bolger, Buddy Ebsen, James Barton, George M. Cohan, Leon Errol, Joe Frisco, George White, Harland Dixon, Jack Donahue, Tom Patricola, and Hal Leroy.

Variants of eccentric dance appeared across the Anglo-American performance circuit, moving between American vaudeville, minstrelsy, Broadway, and British music halls, often overlapping with early eccentric character walking and grotesque dance traditions.
Eccentric dance emerged out of clog and tap traditions under African and exotic dance influences.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Eccentric dance is parent of Clog dance: Eccentric dance developed partly out of clog dancing modified by African dance influences.
Eccentric dance is parent of Tap dance: Traditional tap styles provided the percussive base that eccentric dancers warped with comic acrobatics.
Eccentric dance is child of Charleston: The Charleston drew directly on eccentric moves and improvisational limb isolations during the 1920s craze.
Eccentric dance is child of Shag: Rubberlegging techniques evolved directly into the footwork of swing-era Shag.
